title: chary / wary / weary
core: Three words separated by a single letter, and only two of them are even about caution. *Chary* and *wary* both describe a guarded stance toward something — each takes *of*, and both mark the speaker as unwilling to proceed at face value. *Weary* has no caution in it at all; it belongs to exhaustion. The whole group turns on the fact that all three fit the same frame, "___ of his promises," and each produces a different sentence.

words.nuance: The only one about **rationing**. **Chary** measures how little you hand over — praise, money, detail, trust — so what follows *of* is the thing being withheld, not the thing being feared. It makes the speaker look sparing, even tight-fisted, rather than suspicious: a chary editor gives few compliments, not fewer risks.

Eyes open, aimed at a target. **Wary** carries active distrust of a specific person, offer, or claim — what follows *of* is the suspected danger, not a resource. It withholds nothing and doesn't retreat: you can be wary of a man and still take his deal, watching him the whole time.

The odd one out — no caution, only depletion. The adjective is the tiredness of a long haul, spirit as well as body, and always implies something did the wearing down. **Weary of** is the trap: it means *fed up*, patience spent — the opposite posture from *wary of*, since you've stopped watching because you've stopped caring.

exam_note: In a blank, "wary of" and "weary of" are both grammatical — decide by whether the context supplies a threat to watch (wary) or a long grind to be sick of (weary); pick chary only when the blank governs something being doled out.
